questions.q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution provides for protecting and improving the environment and safeguarding forests and wildlife?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Article 48-A.

Key Points

• Article 48-A of the Indian Constitution specifically deals with the Protection and improvement of the environment and safeguarding of forests and wildlife.
• It falls under Part IV of the Indian Constitution, which encompasses the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP).
• This article was added to the Constitution by the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976.
• According to Article 48-A, the State shall endeavor to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wildlife of the country.
Additional Information

• Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)
• These are guidelines or principles given to the central and state governments of India, to be kept in mind while framing laws and policies.
• They are non-justiciable, meaning their application cannot be enforced by the courts.
• However, they are considered fundamental in the governance of the country, aiming to create social and economic conditions under which citizens can lead a good life.
• 42nd Amendment Act of 1976
• This amendment is also known as the "Mini-Constitution" due to the significant changes it brought to the Indian Constitution.
• It added new directives in the form of Article 48-A and Article 51-A(g) which deals with the protection of the environment and the duty of citizens to protect the environment, respectively.
• It also added ten fundamental duties to the Constitution, emphasizing the responsibility of citizens towards the nation.
• Environmental Protection
• It refers to the practice of protecting the natural environment by individuals, organizations, and governments.
• The primary goal is to conserve natural resources and the existing natural environment and, where possible, to repair damage and reverse trends.
• In India, various laws and regulations have been implemented to ensure environmental protection, including the Environment Protection Act of 1986.
• Forest and Wildlife Conservation
• Conservation of forests and wildlife is crucial for maintaining the ecological balance and biodiversity.
• In India, this is governed by various laws, including the Indian Forest Act, 1927, and the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972.
• These laws aim to regulate and manage forest resources and protect wildlife species from exploitation and extinction.

questions.q: According to Mendeleev's Periodic Table, which elements' properties matched up remarkably well with eka-silicon?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Germanium.

Key Points

• Germanium was the element predicted by Mendeleev and referred to as eka-silicon before its actual discovery.

• Mendeleev predicted the existence of germanium based on his periodic table and its properties matched remarkably well with his predictions.

• Germanium was discovered in 1886 by Clemens Winkler, about 15 years after Mendeleev's prediction.

• The discovery of germanium provided strong support for the accuracy and predictive power of Mendeleev's periodic table.

Additional Information

• Mendeleev's Periodic Table

• Developed by Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869, the periodic table is an arrangement of chemical elements organized by their atomic number, electron configuration, and recurring chemical properties.

• Mendeleev's table predicted the existence and properties of elements that had not yet been discovered.

• His periodic law states that the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic weights.

• Eka-elements

• The term "eka" was used by Mendeleev to denote an element that would be found below another element in the periodic table, following a predicted pattern of properties.

• For example, "eka-silicon" was the name given to the yet-to-be-discovered element germanium.

• Discovery of Germanium

• Germanium was discovered by Clemens Winkler in 1886 in a mineral called argyrodite.

• Winkler's discovery matched Mendeleev's predictions in terms of atomic weight, density, and other properties, thus validating the periodic table.

questions.q: The Atal Innovation Mission was launched in year _.
questions.solution:

Key Points

• The Atal Innovation Mission (AIM) was launched in 2016 as a flagship initiative by the Government of India to promote a culture of innovation and entrepreneurship.

• AIM aims to create an ecosystem of innovation and entrepreneurship at various levels in the country, from schools to higher education institutions and beyond.

• It focuses on fostering innovation and nurturing an innovative mindset through initiatives like Atal Tinkering Labs (ATLs) in schools.

• Additionally, AIM supports the establishment of Atal Incubation Centers (AICs) and aims to encourage startups and small businesses to thrive.

Additional Information

• Atal Tinkering Labs (ATLs)

• ATLs are dedicated workspaces where students (Class 6 to Class 12) learn innovation skills and develop ideas that will go on to transform India.

• These labs are equipped with state-of-the-art tools and technologies like 3D printers, robotics & electronics development tools, IoT & sensors, etc.

• The goal is to foster curiosity, creativity, and imagination in young minds, and inculcate skills such as design mindset, computational thinking, adaptive learning, physical computing, etc.

• Atal Incubation Centers (AICs)

• AIM provides financial support to establish new incubation centers across India.

• AICs aim to foster and support world-class innovation and dynamic startups in various sectors, including social innovation.

• They provide necessary infrastructure and support to startups, such as mentoring, networking, and access to funding.

• Atal New India Challenges

• These challenges aim to foster product innovations and align them to needs of various sectors/ministries.

• The program provides a grant-in-aid of up to Rs. 1 crore for selected innovators/startups to develop their products further.

• Mentor of Change

• This initiative aims to engage leaders who can guide and mentor students in ATLs, entrepreneurs in AICs, and other beneficiaries of AIM programs.

• Mentors provide guidance on various aspects like technology development, business strategy, and market access.

questions.q: Ishwari Prasad is credited to have introduced the _ Gharana of Kathak.
questions.solution:

Key Points

• Ishwari Prasad is credited with the introduction of the Lucknow Gharana of Kathak.

• The Lucknow Gharana is one of the major schools of Kathak dance, and it emphasizes graceful movements and precise footwork.

• It was established in the early 19th century in the court of Nawab Wajid Ali Shah, a patron of the arts.

• The Lucknow Gharana is known for its intricate abhinaya (expression) and delicate movements, making it distinct from other Kathak styles.

Additional Information

• Founded by Bhanuji, it is known for its dynamic spins and extensive use of tatkars (footwork patterns).

• Raigarh Gharana:

• Developed in the princely state of Raigarh, it combines elements of both Jaipur and Lucknow styles.

• It is also known for its musical compositions and rhythm patterns.

• Banaras Gharana:

• It is famous for its expressive and devotional elements.

• Founded by Janakiprasad, this style uses intricate hand movements and facial expressions.

questions.q: Which essential amino acid enhances calcium absorption and also plays an important role in the formation of collagen?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Lysine.

Key Points

• Lysine is an essential amino acid that the body cannot synthesize and must be obtained from the diet.

• Lysine plays a crucial role in enhancing calcium absorption in the body, which is vital for bone health.

• This amino acid is also essential for the formation of collagen, a protein that provides structure to skin, bones, and connective tissues.

• Additionally, lysine is involved in the production of carnitine, a nutrient responsible for converting fatty acids into energy and helping to lower cholesterol levels.

Additional Information

• Essential Amino Acids:

• These are amino acids that cannot be synthesized by the body and must be obtained from the diet.

• There are nine essential amino acids: histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine.

• Calcium Absorption:

• Calcium is a mineral essential for bone health, muscle function, nerve signaling, and blood clotting.

• Vitamin D and certain amino acids, such as lysine, enhance the absorption of calcium in the gut.

• Collagen Formation:

• Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body, providing structure to skin, bones, and connective tissues.

• Lysine is vital for the synthesis of collagen, contributing to tissue repair and skin elasticity.

• Protein Synthesis:

• Proteins are made up of amino acids, which are the building blocks of the body.

• Essential amino acids, including lysine, are crucial for the synthesis of proteins needed for growth, repair, and maintenance of tissues.

questions.q: Who suggested the law that the British Government passed in 1856 to support widow remarriage?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar.

Key Points

• Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar was a prominent social reformer in India who worked tirelessly for the upliftment of women's rights.

• He was instrumental in convincing the British government to pass the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act in 1856, which legalized the remarriage of Hindu widows.

• His efforts were based on rational thinking and deep knowledge of Sanskrit and Hindu scriptures, which he used to argue against the prevailing social norms that restricted widow remarriage.

• Vidyasagar's work had a lasting impact on Indian society, helping to break down oppressive traditions and improve the status of women.

Additional Information

• Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act of 1856:

• This act was a significant social reform that allowed Hindu widows to remarry, which was previously prohibited by societal norms and traditions.

• The act was passed on July 16, 1856, by the British colonial administration in India.

• The law was a result of the extensive campaign led by Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, who used his knowledge of Hindu scriptures to argue that widow remarriage was sanctioned by ancient texts.

• This reform was an important step towards gender equality and improving the social status of women in India.

• Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar:

• Born on September 26, 1820, Vidyasagar was a key figure in the Bengal Renaissance and a well-known scholar, educator, and social reformer.

• He was known for his contributions to education, particularly the introduction of the modern Bengali alphabet and prose.

• Vidyasagar's advocacy for women's rights, including widow remarriage and female education, marked him as a pioneer in the fight for social justice in India.

• He also worked towards simplifying and modernizing the Bengali language, making it more accessible to the common people.

• Other Social Reforms:

• Raja Ram Mohan Roy: Another prominent social reformer, he played a significant role in the abolition of the practice of Sati through the Sati Regulation Act of 1829.

• Keshub Chandra Sen: A leader of the Brahmo Samaj, he also worked towards social and religious reforms in India, including the promotion of women's education.

• Atmaram Pandurang: He was a key figure in the Prarthana Samaj, which aimed at reforming Hindu religious practices and promoting social equality.

questions.q: An organic reaction used to convert an aryl diazonium salt into an aryl halide using a copper(I) halide catalyst is called:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Sandmeyer reaction.

Key Points

• The Sandmeyer reaction is used to convert an aryl diazonium salt into an aryl halide.

• The reaction employs a copper(I) halide catalyst, such as CuCl or CuBr.

• This reaction is particularly useful in the synthesis of various aromatic compounds.

• It is named after the Swiss chemist Traugott Sandmeyer, who discovered it in 1884.

Additional Information

• Finkelstein reaction

• Named after the German chemist Hans Finkelstein.

• It is a halogen exchange reaction used to convert alkyl halides (usually bromides or chlorides) into iodides.

• The reaction employs a metal halide, such as sodium iodide (NaI), in acetone as the solvent.

• This reaction is typically used for the preparation of alkyl iodides.

• Gattermann reaction

• Named after the German chemist Ludwig Gattermann.

• It involves the formylation of aromatic compounds using a mixture of hydrogen cyanide (HCN) and hydrochloric acid (HCl) in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst such as AlCl3.

• This reaction is used to introduce a formyl group (-CHO) into aromatic rings.

• It is often referred to as the Gattermann-Koch reaction when carbon monoxide (CO) is used instead of HCN.

• Balz-Schiemann reaction

• Named after the German chemists Günther Balz and Günther Schiemann.

• It is used to synthesize aryl fluorides from aryl diazonium salts.

• The reaction involves the thermal decomposition of the diazonium tetrafluoroborate salt.

• This method is particularly useful for introducing fluorine into aromatic compounds.

• The Pawn: Moves forward one square, but captures diagonally. On its first move, it can move forward two squares.

• The King: Moves one square in any direction. The objective of the game is to checkmate the opponent's King.

• The chessboard is an 8x8 grid with alternating light and dark squares.

• Each player begins with 16 pieces: one King, one Queen, two Rooks, two Knights, two Bishops, and eight Pawns.

Key Points

• Net Domestic Product (NDP) is derived by subtracting depreciation from the Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

• GDP represents the total monetary value of all finished goods and services produced within a country's borders in a specific time period.

• NDP provides a more accurate reflection of an economy's actual productivity and sustainability by accounting for the depreciation of capital assets.

Additional Information

• Gross Domestic Product (GDP)

• GDP is the total market value of all goods and services produced within a country in a given period.

• It includes all private and public consumption, government outlays, investments, and exports minus imports.

• GDP is a broad measure of a nation's overall economic activity.

• It is often used as an indicator of the economic health of a country.

• Depreciation

• Depreciation is an accounting method of allocating the cost of a tangible or physical asset over its useful life.

• It represents how much of an asset's value has been used up over time.

• Businesses depreciate long-term assets for both tax and accounting purposes.

• Depreciation can affect the net income of a business as it is listed as an expense.

• Net Domestic Product (NDP)

• NDP is an economic indicator that provides a more accurate assessment of an economy's productivity by accounting for depreciation.

• It is calculated as GDP minus depreciation.

• NDP helps in understanding the sustainability of the economic activities by indicating the net addition to the nation's wealth.

• It ensures that the measure of economic performance considers the wear and tear of capital assets.

• Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA)

• NFIA is the difference between the income residents receive from abroad for factor services (like labor and capital) and the income paid to foreign residents for their factor services within the domestic economy.

• It is used in the calculation of Gross National Product (GNP).

• NFIA can indicate the level of economic interaction a country has with the rest of the world.

• A positive NFIA means a country is earning more from its investments abroad than it is paying to foreign investors in the domestic market.

questions.q: The salaries of P and Q together amount to ₹9,60,000. P and Q save 64% and 44%, respectively of their individual salaries. If P's expenditure is 1.5 times Q's expenditure, then what is the ratio of P's salary to Q's salary?
questions.solution:
Shortcut Trick

P's expenditure % = 100% − 64% = 36%

Q's expenditure % = 100% − 44% = 56%

Given, P's expenditure = 1.5 × Q's expenditure

⇒ 36% of P = 1.5 × 56% of Q

⇒ P / Q = (1.5 × 56) / 36 = 84 / 36 = 7 / 3

∴ The correct answer is 7 : 3.

Alternate Method

Given:

⇒ Total Salary of P and Q = ₹9,60,000

⇒ Savings of P = 64% of P's Salary

⇒ Savings of Q = 44% of Q's Salary

⇒ Expenditure of P = 1.5 × Expenditure of Q



Calculations:

⇒ Expenditure of P = (100 − 64)% of P's Salary = 36% of P's Salary

⇒ Expenditure of Q = (100 − 44)% of Q's Salary = 56% of Q's Salary

⇒ According to the given condition, 36% of P's Salary = 1.5 × 56% of Q's Salary

⇒ (36 / 100) × P = 1.5 × (56 / 100) × Q

⇒ 36 × P = 84 × Q

⇒ P / Q = 84 / 36

⇒ P / Q = 7 / 3

∴ The correct answer is 7 : 3.

Additional Information

Income, Expenditure and Savings

Total Income is the sum of total expenditure and total savings: Income = Expenditure + Savings.

Redundant Data Trick

When calculating ratios or percentage relationships, exact values (such as the combined sum of ₹9,60,000) are often unnecessary and skipping them saves valuable time.

Ratio Scaling Rule

If a × A = b × B, then A : B = b : a. This cross-multiplication principle quickly converts algebraic equations into straightforward ratios by swapping the coefficients.

questions.q: It is always possible to draw a circle passing through  non-collinear points in a plane.
questions.solution:

According to fundamental geometric principles, exactly one unique circle can be drawn passing through three non-collinear points.

Any three non-collinear points form a triangle, and the center of the unique circle passing through them is the circumcenter of this triangle.

The circumcenter is geometrically determined by the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the sides, ensuring it is equidistant from all three vertices.

Hence, 3 non-collinear points are always required and strictly sufficient to define a single circle.

∴ The correct answer is 3.

Concept Used:

A circle is geometrically defined as the locus of all points in a plane that are at an equal distance (radius) from a fixed center point.

Shortcut Trick

If xⁿ + 1/xⁿ = 2 for any positive value of x, then x must be 1.

Given, a³ + 1/a³ = 2, which directly implies a = 1.

⇒ a + 1/a = 1 + 1/1 = 2

Given:

a³ + 1/a³ = 2 (where a > 0)

(a + 1/a)³ = a³ + 1/a³ + 3(a + 1/a)

Calculation:

Let (a + 1/a) = k

Substitute the given values into the algebraic identity:

⇒ k³ = 2 + 3k

⇒ k³ − 3k − 2 = 0

⇒ k³ − k − 2k − 2 = 0

⇒ k(k² − 1) − 2(k + 1) = 0

⇒ k(k − 1)(k + 1) − 2(k + 1) = 0

⇒ (k + 1)[k(k − 1) − 2] = 0

⇒ (k + 1)(k² − k − 2) = 0

⇒ (k + 1)(k − 2)(k + 1) = 0

⇒ (k + 1)²(k − 2) = 0

This gives k = −1 or k = 2.

Since it is given that a > 0, the sum (a + 1/a) must be a positive number.

⇒ k = 2

⇒ a + 1/a = 2

∴ The correct answer is 2.

questions.q: Nihira is 25 years old and Punith is 30 years old. How many years ago was the ratio of their ages 3 : 4?
questions.solution:
Shortcut Trick

The difference in ages is always constant over time. Difference in present ages = 30 − 25 = 5 years.

In the past, the ratio was 3 : 4. Difference in ratio parts = 4 − 3 = 1 part.

So, 1 part = 5 years.

Past age of Nihira = 3 parts = 3 × 5 = 15 years.

Number of years ago = Present age − Past age = 25 − 15 = 10 years.

∴ The correct answer is 10 years.

Alternate Method



Given:

Present age of Nihira = 25 years

Present age of Punith = 30 years

Let the required number of years ago be x.

Calculation:

⇒ x years ago, Nihira's age = (25 − x) years

⇒ x years ago, Punith's age = (30 − x) years

According to the given condition, their age ratio was 3 : 4.

⇒ (25 − x) / (30 − x) = 3 / 4

Cross-multiplying the equation:

⇒ 4 × (25 − x) = 3 × (30 − x)

⇒ 100 − 4x = 90 − 3x

⇒ 100 − 90 = 4x − 3x

⇒ x = 10

∴ The correct answer is 10 years.

Additional Information

Constant Age Difference Rule

The difference between the ages of two individuals remains exactly the same regardless of the time period (past, present, or future).

Ratio of Ages in Future/Past

If the present ages are A and B, then 't' years ago, their age ratio was (A − t) : (B − t), and 't' years hence, it will be (A + t) : (B + t).

Cross-Multiplication Method

When comparing two ratios at two different points in time, you can directly equate the differences of cross products to the time gap to find the 1-unit multiplier quickly.

questions.q: Find the values of 'a' and 'b' for which the system of equations 3x + y = 3 and (a - b)x + (a + b)y = 3a + b - 3 has infinite solutions.
questions.solution:
Shortcut Trick

For a system to have infinite solutions, a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂

⇒ 3 / (a − b) = 1 / (a + b) = 3 / (3a + b − 3)

From 1st & 2nd terms: 3a + 3b = a − b ⇒ 2a = −4b ⇒ a = −2b

From 2nd & 3rd terms: 3a + b − 3 = 3a + 3b ⇒ 2b = −3 ⇒ b = −3/2

Substituting b into a: a = −2 × (−3/2) = 3

∴ The correct answer is a = 3, b = −3/2.

Alternate Method

Given:

System of equations:

3x + y = 3

(a − b)x + (a + b)y = 3a + b − 3

Formula Used:

For a system of linear equations a₁x + b₁y = c₁ and a₂x + b₂y = c₂ to have infinite solutions:

a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂

Calculations:

⇒ Comparing the given equations with standard form:

⇒ a₁ = 3, b₁ = 1, c₁ = 3

⇒ a₂ = a − b, b₂ = a + b, c₂ = 3a + b − 3

⇒ Applying the condition for infinite solutions:

⇒ 3 / (a − b) = 1 / (a + b) = 3 / (3a + b − 3)

Taking the first two parts of the equation:

⇒ 3 / (a − b) = 1 / (a + b)

⇒ 3(a + b) = 1(a − b)

⇒ 3a + 3b = a − b

⇒ 3a − a = −b − 3b

⇒ 2a = −4b

⇒ a = −2b --- (Equation 1)

Taking the second and third parts of the equation:

⇒ 1 / (a + b) = 3 / (3a + b − 3)

⇒ 1(3a + b − 3) = 3(a + b)

⇒ 3a + b − 3 = 3a + 3b

⇒ 3a − 3a − 3 = 3b − b

⇒ −3 = 2b

⇒ b = −3/2

Substitute the value of b in Equation 1:

⇒ a = −2 × (−3/2)

⇒ a = 3

∴ The correct answer is a = 3, b = −3/2.

Additional Information

Condition for Unique Solution

A system of equations a₁x + b₁y = c₁ and a₂x + b₂y = c₂ has a unique solution (intersecting lines) if a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂.

Condition for No Solution

A system of equations has no solution (parallel lines) if a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂.

Condition for Infinite Solutions

A system has infinitely many solutions (coincident lines) if a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂.

questions.q: Suppose P starts walking at a speed of 8 km/h. After 8 hours B started travelling on a bicycle at a speed of 24 km/h. The distance from the starting B can catch P is:
questions.solution:
Shortcut Trick

Head start distance covered by P in 8 hours = 8 × 8 = 64 km.

Relative speed of B (moving in the same direction) = 24 − 8 = 16 km/h.

Time taken by B to catch P = 64 ÷ 16 = 4 hours.

Distance from the starting point = B's speed × time = 24 × 4 = 96 km.

∴ The correct answer is 96 km.

Alternate Method

Given:

Speed of P = 8 km/h

Speed of B = 24 km/h

Head start time for P = 8 hours



Formula Used:

Distance = Speed × Time

Relative Speed (same direction) = Speed of B − Speed of P

Catch-up Time = Initial Gap Distance ÷ Relative Speed

Calculations:

⇒ Distance covered by P before B starts = 8 × 8 = 64 km

⇒ This 64 km is the gap that B needs to cover to catch P.

⇒ Relative speed of B to P = 24 − 8 = 16 km/h

⇒ Time taken by B to close the gap = 64 ÷ 16 = 4 hours

⇒ Distance from the starting point = B's speed × Time taken

⇒ Distance = 24 × 4 = 96 km

∴ The correct answer is 96 km.

Additional Information

Relative Speed (Same Direction)

When two objects travel in the same direction, their relative speed is the difference between their individual speeds: Relative Speed = S₁ − S₂.

Catch-up Time Formula

The time required to overtake or catch a head-start object is given by: Time = Initial Gap Distance ÷ Relative Speed.

Distance by Ratio Method

When the travel time is constant for two moving bodies, the ratio of the distances they cover is directly proportional to the ratio of their speeds: D₁/D₂ = S₁/S₂.

questions.q: Ramesh purchased 130 books at the rate of ₹200 each and sold half of them at the rate of ₹300 each, one-fifth of them at the rate of ₹350 each and the rest at the cost price. Find his profit percentage.

⇒ Profit % = (10,400 ÷ 26,000) × 100 = 40%

∴ The correct answer is 40%.

Additional Information

Weighted Average Profit/Loss

When different parts of a total quantity are sold at different profit or loss percentages, the net profit/loss % is the weighted sum of individual percentages.

Profit and Loss Formulas

Profit = Selling Price (SP) − Cost Price (CP). Profit percentage is always calculated on the base of Cost Price: Profit % = (Profit ÷ CP) × 100.
